title: Shiphrah and Puah (Exodus 1:15–21)
hookLine: two midwives quietly refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the baby boys

lines: IF IT'S A BOY, KILL IT.
cards: The labor isn't working; the Israelites keep growing. So Pharaoh does something worse. He calls in two women, midwives, the ones who help the Hebrew mothers give birth.
And the text, which leaves out so many names, gives us theirs: Shiphrah and Puah. Pharaoh's order is simple and monstrous. When you deliver a Hebrew woman's baby, look.
If it's a boy, kill it. If it's a girl, let her live. Two midwives, alone, facing the king of Egypt.

teach.b: They don't argue. They don't lead a protest. They just don't do it.

"But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." Feared God: the Hebrew means something like reverence, a sense that there's something above the king.
Pharaoh calls them back. Why have you let the boys live? Their answer is brilliant.
The Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women.

teach.h: THEY GIVE BIRTH BEFORE WE ARRIVE.
teach.b: They're lively, full of life; they give birth before the midwife even gets there. Pharaoh can't check.
They walk out alive, and the text says God dealt well with the midwives, and made them houses: families, households of their own. Now, a puzzle.
The Hebrew can be read two ways: Hebrew midwives, or midwives to the Hebrews. If they're Hebrew women, they're protecting their own people.

Some medieval commentators, like Abarbanel, suggested they were Egyptian women protecting someone else's babies. One opinion in the Talmud says they were Moses' own mother and sister, under other names.
The text doesn't settle it. What it does make plain: the first people in the book of Exodus to stand up to Pharaoh aren't prophets or soldiers.
They're two working women with a job to do, who wouldn't do it wrong.
Some modern writers call it civil disobedience. Quiet, practical, and brave.

how: Jewish teaching often holds up Shiphrah and Puah as models of moral courage, and the Talmud credits righteous women with the redemption from Egypt.

o: a woman who warned the Hebrews to flee Egypt
a midwife who refused Pharaoh's order to kill
an Egyptian queen who pleaded for the slaves

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: they give birth before we arrive

s: they quietly didn't do it, then gave him an answer he couldn't check.
the Torah gives the midwives' names
Shiphrah and Puah, while it leaves Pharaoh unnamed.
everyone agrees the midwives were Hebrew
the Hebrew can be read either way; Abarbanel suggested they were Egyptian.

games.q: you're a midwife. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, has ordered you to kill every Hebrew baby boy you deliver. what do you do?
games.why: they let the boys live, and when Pharaoh asks why, they say the Hebrew women give birth before the midwife arrives.

practice: Think of something you're expected to go along with that you know isn't right: a joke at someone's expense, a shortcut at work that cheats a customer, a bit of gossip you're about to pass on. It doesn't have to be dramatic.
Picture yourself just not doing it, quietly, the way the midwives did.

wordCard.voice: Shiphrah, one of the two midwives Pharaoh ordered to kill the baby boys, who quietly refused. The Talmud links her name to making beautiful.

orig.note: Hebrew: Shiphrah and Puah. the Talmud links Shiphrah to a word for making beautiful.

carryVoice: Your line: the midwives said no. No protest, no speech, just a quiet no. Day seventy-eight.
